proof:
# Weighted base reflection can retain less than one quarter in two dimensions

The one-dimensional median-reflection theorem does not extend to arbitrary log-concave weights on a lattice-convex polygon. The failure persists for a strictly positive affine radius profile raised to an integer power, and hence for actual compatible full-dimensional convex fibers.

## 1. The complete twelve-point lattice polygon

Let

    Q=conv{(0,0),(1,0),(1,4),(-1,4),(-1,3)}
     ={(u,v): -1<=u<=1, 0<=v<=4, 3u+v>=0}.

Its complete integer support is

    P=Q intersect Z^2
     = {(0,v),(1,v): v=0,1,2,3,4} union {(-1,3),(-1,4)}.  (1)

The displayed inequalities prove both descriptions and lattice completeness directly. In particular P has row counts `2,2,2,3,3` at heights `0,1,2,3,4`. All five vertices are integer points.

Give every point at height v the weight t_v, where

    t_0>=t_1>=t_2>=t_3>=t_4>0.

The total mass is

    M=2(t_0+t_1+t_2)+3(t_3+t_4).                       (2)

For every integer center j define the reflected base retention

    B(j)=sum_(p in P) min(w_p,w_(2j-p)),

where weights outside P are zero. The following table exhausts all centers in P. Each formula follows by listing the actual reflected partners and taking the weight at the larger of their heights.

| Centers j | B(j) |
| --- | --- |
| `(0,0),(1,0)` | `t_0` |
| `(0,1),(1,1)` | `t_1+2t_2` |
| `(0,2)` | `t_2+4t_3+4t_4` |
| `(1,2)` | `t_2+2t_3+2t_4` |
| `(-1,3)` | `t_3` |
| `(0,3)` | `3t_3+4t_4` |
| `(1,3)` | `t_3+2t_4` |
| `(-1,4),(1,4)` | `t_4` |
| `(0,4)` | `3t_4` |

Every row after the third is bounded by that third row or by t_0. Thus

    max_j B(j)=max{t_0, t_1+2t_2, t_2+4t_3+4t_4}.      (3)

There are no additional nonzero centers outside P: a positive reflected pair would express its integer center as the midpoint of two points of Q, hence place that center in P. Therefore (3) is the maximum over ALL integer centers, not merely over selected candidates.

## 2. A log-affine counterexample

Set `t_v=2^(-v)`. The function `2^(-v)` restricted to Q and extended by zero is log-concave, and its positive sampled support is exactly P. Equations (2)–(3) give

    M=65/16,       max_j B(j)=1,
    max_j B(j)/M=16/65<1/4.                            (4)

The maximum is attained at exactly `(0,0),(1,0),(0,1),(1,1),(0,2)`. The gap from one quarter is `1/260`.

This is not a product distribution on a box, so it does not contradict the product corollary of the one-dimensional theorem.

## 3. A rational positive affine-root counterexample in dimension 14

For an actual concave-root volume profile take

    d=14,       r(u,v)=21-v,       w_(u,v)=(21-v)^14.    (5)

The radius is affine, positive everywhere on Q, and ranges from 17 to 21. Write

    A=21^14=3243919932521508681,
    B=20^14=1638400000000000000,
    C=19^14=799006685782884121,
    D=18^14=374813367582081024,
    E=17^14=168377826559400929.

The two nontrivial competitors in (3) are strictly below A, with exact integer certificates

    A-B-2C       =7506560955740439>0,
    A-C-4D-4E    =272148470172696748>0.                 (6)

On the other hand,

    M=2(A+B+C)+3(D+E)=12992226819033231463,
    M-4A=16547088947196739>0.                           (7)

Consequently

    max_(j in Z^2) B(j)=A<M/4.                          (8)

Only the two centers `(0,0),(1,0)` attain A. All arithmetic in (5)–(8) is integral; the normalized ratio is approximately `0.2496815964`, but that approximation is not used in the proof.

## 4. Exact realization by compatible convex fibers

Choose any full-dimensional convex body K in R^14 of volume one, for example `K=[-1/2,1/2]^14`, and form

    C_body = {(u,v,x): (u,v) in Q, x in (21-v)K}.        (9)

This is a compact full-dimensional convex body in `R^2 x R^14`. To check convexity directly, if `x_i=r_i k_i` with `k_i in K`, then for a convex combination with radius `r=sum lambda_i r_i>0`,

    sum lambda_i x_i
      =r sum (lambda_i r_i/r) k_i in rK.

Every actual integer fiber is exactly `(21-v)K` at `(u,v) in P`, so its volume is the weight (5). There are no omitted positive integer fibers. The same calculation proves every sampled Minkowski inclusion, with equality because the common radius is affine.

Moreover `C_body=conv(C_body intersect (Z^2 x R^14))`. Indeed represent a base point by the integer vertices of Q. For `x=r(p)k`, use the same k at every corresponding vertex fiber and the affine identity for r. This realizes `(p,x)` as a convex combination of actual mixed source points.

For the centered cube choice, all fiber centroids are zero, so even an affine centroid graph does not repair the asserted BASE retention bound. It remains a counterexample to that proposed sufficient invariant, not to the mixed-integer depth bound. For clarity, the own central point of either heaviest cube already supplies absolute cap mass at least `A/2`. Since `M<(9/2)A` and `Gamma_14<=Gamma_2=4/9`, this is strictly larger than `Gamma_14 M/4`. Thus the actual body explicitly satisfies the desired depth target despite (8).

## 5. Why the one-dimensional pairing proof does not tensorize

The one-dimensional proof uses four collinear indices: the inner pair lies on the segment between the outer pair and has the same sum. Log-concavity controls their product. Coordinatewise replacement in two dimensions need not produce a pair on that segment.

Here take `p=(-1,3)` and `q=(1,0)`, both in P. The opposite rectangle corners `r=(-1,0)` and `s=(1,3)` have the same vector sum and lie in the coordinate bounding rectangle, but r is outside Q. Thus

    w_p w_q>0=w_r w_s.

Convex support and ordinary log-concavity impose no rectangular four-point inequality of the required kind. The exact counterexamples above show that this is a substantive obstruction to the general extension.

The standard-library verifier `../assets/pk-nov6/computations/verify_nonproduct_weighted_reflection_counterexample.py` certifies the lattice support, all twelve reflection rows, both strict examples, and the actual-body scalar constants. No optimization over approximate cap normals enters this certificate.
